LHX.sentence: L3Harris is down a touch and its profit margins are running below their usual level, but steady defense spending means the underlying business hasn't really changed.

ASML.sentence: ASML has drifted down about 20% from its high, which is just the normal up-and-down for them — they're still the only company on earth making a certain essential chipmaking machine, and demand for it isn't going anywhere.

LIN.sentence: Linde is having a quiet stretch — they supply industrial gases under long contracts and nudge prices up a little each quarter, and that steady grind is the whole story with this one.

MSFT.sentence: Microsoft is quiet and actually holding up better than most of the other big tech names during a wobbly month — the cloud-and-AI story just keeps grinding along without drama.

TMO.sentence: Thermo Fisher is flat, but biotech funding has been soft for a while, and since that funding eventually becomes orders for its lab equipment, that softness may show up in its sales a couple of quarters down the road.

CVX.sentence: Chevron fell about 4.5% as oil eased, which is simply the war-driven price spike draining out rather than anything going wrong — its profits look swollen right now because fighting near Iran has pushed oil far above the ordinary price it actually plans its business around.

NOW.sentence: ServiceNow has dropped sharply — down nearly half from its high and far worse than its peers — on no obvious company-specific problem, while big companies and government agencies keep signing on for its workflow and AI tools under long multi-year contracts.

GLNCY.sentence: Glencore barely budged even as copper prices fell sharply, because its giant commodity-trading arm tends to make money in choppy markets and cushioned the mining side.

MLM.sentence: Martin Marietta rose about 3%, and the price it gets for a ton of crushed stone is still creeping up nicely — the headline price looked soft only because of what mix of products they happened to sell, not because the business is weakening.

KOF.sentence: Coca-Cola FEMSA eased back as the Mexican peso weakened, which quietly shrinks the value of its mostly-peso earnings when converted to dollars — a currency headwind rather than a problem with selling Coke.

UBER.sentence: Uber ticked up, and people keep booking more and more rides and food orders through it — fast enough that there's still no sign the self-driving car companies are pulling business away.

AMKBY.sentence: Maersk, the Danish container-shipping giant, is trading for less than it would cost to rebuild its fleet of ships — an unusually cheap price for a company that's a decent barometer of global trade.

MA.sentence: Mastercard is barely moved — people keep tapping their cards more than ever and it collects a tiny toll each time, so nothing is really happening here beyond the usual steady grind.

ISRG.sentence: The da Vinci surgical-robot maker is down about 30% from its high, lagging other medical-device companies, which looks more like nervous selling than any real sign hospitals are doing fewer robot-assisted surgeries.

NVDA.sentence: Nvidia fell again, down sharply from its high the day before its results, mostly because two of its biggest customers (Google's parent and Amazon) showed they're borrowing to pay for all the computing gear they buy — nothing changed at Nvidia itself, but whether those customers can keep spending is the whole question.
